title: Detection of Question-Answer Pairs in Email Conversations
research_question: Can question-answer pairs in asynchronous email threads be detected for summarization more effectively by combining automatic question detection with thread-structure-aware answer pairing than by relying on lexical similarity alone?
methodology: The authors first trained RIPPER rules for interrogative-question detection using 5,000 positive and 5,000 negative SWITCHBOARD/DAMSL examples and tested the detector on manually selected ACM email questions and statements. For answer detection, they annotated question-answer links in a corpus of approximately 300 email threads containing about 1,000 messages from a Columbia University ACM student organization and represented messages as paragraph-level discourse segments. They trained RIPPER classifiers with lexical, positional, candidate-set, and email-thread structural features and evaluated them with five-fold cross-validation against a cosine-similarity baseline. They additionally divided questions according to whether they had at most two or more than two candidate answer segments.

key_findings.finding: Thread-structure and candidate-context features substantially improved answer-pair detection over lexical similarity alone: on the Union annotation set, F1 increased from 0.503 with cosine similarity to 0.656 with the full feature set.

Alignment became markedly harder as the number of plausible answer segments increased: the full model reached F1 0.899 for questions with at most two candidate answers but 0.625 for questions with more candidates.
Training separate classifiers for low- and high-candidate cases and combining their predictions produced F1 0.730, compared with 0.656 for the unsplit Union data.

A heuristic that split initially missed utterances at commas and re-applied the question rules to the first and last phrases raised interrogative-question recall from 0.56 to 0.72 while precision remained 0.96, increasing F1 from 0.70 to 0.82.

The annotations included highlighted questions for which no corresponding answer was present in the thread, but answer-pair training instances were constructed only for questions that had a marked answer.
Annotator agreement was higher for linking answers to an identified question segment than for identifying question segments themselves, with reported kappa values of 0.81 and 0.68 respectively.

limitations: The email corpus is small and comes from a single student-organization setting, limiting evidence about generalization to workplace or other email domains.
Questions without marked answers were not included in the answer-pair classifier's candidate training instances, so unanswered-question detection was not evaluated as a modeled outcome.
Messages were segmented primarily by paragraphs, which is too coarse to represent proposition-level partial replies when a paragraph contains several requests or propositions.
Automatic detection of declarative-form questions and rhetorical questions was explicitly left for future work.
The two annotators had completed different portions of the corpus at the time of the study, so the annotation set was still incomplete.
The study did not evaluate whether adding detected question-answer pairs actually improved downstream email summaries.
raw_claims: About one fifth of the email threads in the corpus primarily involved question-answer exchanges.
Email participants can pursue several questions in parallel because responses are asynchronous.
Reply headers do not guarantee that the content of a message answers the immediately preceding message.
An answer can occur several messages after the question that motivated it.
Questions and their answers can have little lexical overlap.
The system treats paragraphs as discourse segments because different issues are often addressed in separate paragraphs.
Thread-structural features improved recall relative to a cosine-similarity-only baseline.
Questions with many candidate answer segments were substantially more difficult to align than questions with few candidates.
Some annotated questions had no corresponding answer anywhere in the thread.
The reported system did not automatically handle declarative-form or rhetorical questions.
